Consider a function $f(t)$ such that its Laplace transform is $L{f(t)}=F(s)$ for $s>{s}_{0}.$ Suppose we wish to find $L{{e}^{2t}f(t)}.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below. By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write 

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{2t}f(t)} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-1}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-2}}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={{field-3}}\,\text{for}\,{{field-4}}.\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.problem:
Consider a function $m(t)$ such that its Laplace transform is $L{m(t)}=M(s)$ for $s>{s}_{0}.$ Suppose we wish to find $L{{e}^{-8t}m(t)}.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below.By definition of the Laplace transform, we can write 

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{-8t}m(t)} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-1}}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{{field-2}}\,m(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={{field-3}}\,\text{for}\,{{field-4}}.\end{aligned}
$$
feedback.worked_solution:
Starting from the definition of the Laplace transform, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{{e}^{-8t}m(t)} & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\cdot {e}^{-8t}\,m(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s+8)t}\,m(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall that $M(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,m(t)\,\text{d}t,$ where $s>{s}_{0}.$ Therefore, 

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-(s+8)t}\,m(t)\,\text{d}t=M(s+8),
$$

where 

$$
s+8>{s}_{0}\,⇒\,s>{s}_{0}-8.
$$
